summary: This unit teaches you to mark out electrical work accurately from drawings: datum lines and heights, box and accessory positions, conduit and trunking routes, ceiling light grids, outdoor cable routes, and cut-outs and holes in enclosures, gland plates and panel back plates. You will learn to choose and check the tools, do the calculations, mark clearly, deal with differences between the drawing and the building, and lead and check a team's set-out before anything is drilled or cut.

blocks.p: Every hole drilled, chase cut and box fixed on an electrical job starts as a mark. A mark in the wrong place means a box out of line with its neighbours, a light that misses the centre of a room, a cut-out a meter falls through, or a drill bit through a hidden pipe. Putting it right costs far more than marking it right. At Level 3 you set out from drawings and specifications, decide the best method and tools for each job, do the calculations, check others' marking, and record what was done.

Give everyone the same references, share the work, and check it before cutting starts.

blocks.note: Most Jamaican buildings are reinforced concrete and concrete block, with conduit cast into slabs and run in block walls before plastering. Once the plaster is on, a mistake in a box position is expensive to fix, and drilling a slab can hit reinforcing steel or a buried conduit. Mark carefully, check twice, and drill once.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing to mark out: documents, site check and safety

head: Document
What you take from it
rows: Drawings (plans, elevations, sections, panel drawings)
Positions, routes, dimensions, the symbol key, the scale, and the revision letter and date
Specification
Mounting heights, materials, tolerances, fixing centres, burial depths, and workmanship rules
Schedules
Lists of fittings, outlets, circuits and their heights or types
Makers' data sheets
Cut-out sizes, hole sizes, fixing centres and clearances for each device

ul: Check the **revision** of every drawing against the site's drawing register. Work only from the current revision, and take superseded copies out of use.

Use the **written dimensions**. Scale (measure) the drawing only where no dimension is given, and check a known dimension first: a copy printed at a different size no longer matches its written scale.

If the drawing and the specification disagree (for example a height of 1 200 mm on the drawing and 1 100 mm in the specification), do not choose for yourself. Ask the supervisor or designer which is right, and record the answer.

blocks.p: Compare the building with the drawing before you mark anything. Note doors, windows, beams, columns and walls that are in different places or sizes, other services already installed, and anything that will get in the way. A wall built 300 mm away from where the drawing shows it changes every position measured from it. When you find a difference, stop marking that part, measure and photograph it, and ask the supervisor for direction.

blocks.h: Hazards when marking out, and their controls

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Work at height (ceilings, high walls)
Mark on the floor and transfer positions up with a plumb laser or plumb bob where you can. Otherwise use a podium or stepladder in good condition on firm ground, with a second person nearby.
Hidden cables, conduits and pipes
Check the drawings, scan with a detector, and treat existing circuits as live until they are isolated and proved dead.
Dust from drilling and chasing concrete and block
On-tool dust extraction or water, eye protection, and respiratory protection as the risk assessment says. The fine silica dust can cause lasting lung disease.
Laser beams
Never look into the beam; set lasers so the beam is not at the eye level of people walking past; use the laser class the site allows.
Trips from tapes, string lines, pegs and tools
Keep walkways clear; fence or flag pegs and lines outdoors.
Other trades working nearby, and site traffic
Agree areas and times with them; wear hard hat, high-visibility vest and safety boots on site.
Sharp sheet-metal edges and swarf
Handle cut edges with care; deburr; clear swarf with a brush or vacuum, never by hand or by blowing.

sections.title: Reference points: datums, level and plumb

blocks.p: A **datum** is a known reference from which other measurements are taken. On a building site the key datum is a level line marked round each room at a set height above the **finished floor level (FFL)**: the level of the floor once screed and tiles are laid. The builder gives a reference height, often a mark on a column or wall such as 'FFL + 1 000'. You mark the datum line from it and write its height beside it, for example 'datum 1 000 mm above FFL', so every trade reads heights from the same line.

ul: Measure every height **from the datum**, never from the rough floor slab. The slab may slope, and screed and tiles will raise the finished floor later.
Heights above FFL become distances from the datum: with the datum at 1 000 mm, a switch at 1 250 mm is 250 mm above the datum; an outlet at 400 mm is 600 mm below it.
Carry the datum from room to room from a common point (for example a mark beside a doorway), and check it against the builder's reference at the far end of the building.
On enclosures and panels, the datum is usually one machined or straight **edge** (a 'datum edge'), and all positions are measured from it and from a second edge at 90° to it.

blocks.p: The specification always decides. Common figures are switch centres about 1 200 mm to 1 400 mm above FFL, general outlets about 300 mm to 450 mm, kitchen worktop outlets about 150 mm to 200 mm above the worktop, and outlets for wall-mounted equipment where the equipment needs them.

Slow; sways in wind; needs a still line
Water level (clear tube filled with water)

Slow; air bubbles in the tube give false readings; needs two people
Chalk line
Snapping a long straight line between two marks on a wall or floor
Does not find level by itself; can smudge or wash off; must be pulled tight and snapped straight out from the surface

blocks.h: Checking that the tools are true

ul: **Line laser:** check it the way its maker describes, typically by marking its line on two facing walls, turning the laser through 180° (or moving it from one wall to the other) and marking again. If the marks disagree by more than the maker allows, send it for adjustment. Check it regularly and after any knock or fall.
**Spirit level:** place it on a firm, nearly level surface, read the bubble, turn it end for end on exactly the same spot and read again. If the bubble sits in the same place both ways, it is true.
**Tape measure:** check the hook against a steel rule. A bent or loose hook gives a constant error on every measurement.
**Square:** draw a line along the blade, flip the square over, draw again from the same point: the lines should coincide.

blocks.h: Plumb, not 'parallel to the door frame'

blocks.p: Door frames, columns and walls are seldom perfectly vertical. A conduit drop marked parallel to a frame that leans will lean too, and the eye picks it up at once against a true box or fitting. Mark vertical lines with a plumb laser, plumb bob or level.

rows: Tape measure (5 m, 8 m, 30 m)

Check the hook; pull it straight and flat; read square to the blade; for long distances hold it tight and level

Try square or combination square
Lines at 90° to an edge; checking corners
Hold the stock firmly against the datum edge

Close the jaws and check it reads zero first
Scriber
A fine, lasting line on bare metal
Do not scribe painted surfaces that will stay on show: it breaks the coating and invites rust
Fine marker or pencil on masking tape

Masking tape protects the paint and shows the marks clearly

A small dimple so a drill starts exactly on the mark

blocks.h: What a good mark looks like

ul: **Clear and unambiguous:** a box is marked with its outline and two crossing centre lines, not just a dot.
**Labelled:** what it is (S for switch, O for outlet, the circuit or type), and its height if useful.
**Consistent:** everyone in the team uses the same symbols and the same edge of the datum line.
**Lasting long enough:** it must survive until the item is fixed, but not mark finished surfaces permanently.

**Measured from one reference:** take every position along a wall from the same starting point ('running dimensions'), not from the last mark. Measuring each from the one before carries every small error on and lets it grow.

blocks.p: Before marking a fixing or drilling position, think about what may be behind it. In British practice, cables in walls are expected in **safe zones**: strips running vertically and horizontally in line with an accessory, and within about 150 mm of the top of a wall or a corner. In Jamaica most cables run in conduit cast into blockwork and slabs, and routes may not follow any zone. So:

ul: Treat any spot directly above, below or beside an existing outlet or switch as a likely cable route.
Check the drawings and any as-built records, and ask other trades about their pipes.
Scan with a detector, remembering it is only a guide.
Where the risk is high, isolate the circuits that could be there, or open up carefully by hand.

blocks.p: Work every set-out sum on paper first, show the working, and check it before you mark. Keep all dimensions in millimetres to avoid decimal slips.

Real size = drawing measurement × scale number. On a 1:20 drawing, 37 mm is 37 × 20 = 740 mm on site. On a 1:100 drawing, 1 mm on paper stands for 100 mm on site. If an A1 drawing is printed on A3 paper, every length is halved, so a drawing marked 1:50 is really about 1:100 on that print: use the written dimensions or the printed scale bar.

Distance from datum = required height above FFL − datum height above FFL. A plus answer is above the datum, a minus answer below. Datum 1 000 mm: a box at 1 400 mm is 400 mm above; a box at 300 mm is 700 mm below.

head: Layout
Spacing
Example: 4 lights along 12 m
rows: Half a space at each end (the usual layout for even lighting)
length ÷ number of items; first item at half a space
A full space at each end
length ÷ (number of items + 1)
Items at both ends, or at set distances from the ends
(length between the end items) ÷ (number of items − 1)
End lights 1 m from the walls: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 m

blocks.note: Count the **gaps**, not the items. Items in a row with one at each end have one gap fewer than items; with a full space at each end they have one gap more.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: To space fixings along trunking, conduit or tray no more than a maximum distance apart, with fixings a set distance from each end: number of gaps = (length − the two end distances) ÷ maximum spacing, **rounded up**; fixings = gaps + 1; actual spacing = (length − the two end distances) ÷ gaps. **Example:** a 3 m length, fixings at most 500 mm apart, 75 mm from each end: (3 000 − 150) ÷ 500 = 5.7, so 6 gaps and 7 fixings, spaced 2 850 ÷ 6 = 475 mm apart.

To centre an item of width w on a space of width W, the gap each side is (W − w) ÷ 2. **Example:** a 350 mm DIN rail centred on a 500 mm back plate starts (500 − 350) ÷ 2 = 75 mm in from each edge. Often it is quicker and more accurate to mark the centre line first and measure half the item's width each way.

ul: **3-4-5:** a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 units has a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides. Any multiple works: 0.6-0.8-1.0 m, 1.5-2.0-2.5 m, 2.4-3.2-4.0 m. Use the biggest that fits: a bigger triangle gives a more accurate angle.

If the diagonal is **too long**, the angle is more than 90°; if it is **too short**, the angle is less than 90°. Move the far mark round (keeping its distance from the corner) until the diagonal is right.
**Equal diagonals:** a rectangle is square when its two diagonals are equal. Use this to check a ceiling grid or a panel layout.
**Pythagoras:** for any right-angled triangle, diagonal = √(a² + b²).

blocks.p: To set out an angle from a baseline, use the tangent: offset = distance along the baseline × tan(angle). At 1 000 mm along, a 20° line is 1 000 × 0.364 = 364 mm out. For a **conduit offset** (two equal bends to step round an obstacle), the distance between the bends = offset depth ÷ sin(bend angle):

head: Bend angle
Multiply the offset depth by
Example: 100 mm offset
rows: 576 mm between bends
261 mm
200 mm
141 mm
115 mm

blocks.p: Smaller angles give a gentler offset that is easier to draw cables through, but need more length. Follow the bender's instructions for where to put each mark on the bender.

ul: **Finishes:** a box must finish flush with the finished surface. If 12 mm of plaster goes on the blockwork, the box front is set 12 mm out from the block; if tiles and adhesive then go over the plaster, add their thickness too.
**Recess depth:** depth to cut = box depth − how far it stands proud. A 35 mm box that must stand 12 mm proud needs a 23 mm recess.
**Clearances:** devices on an enclosure door must clear parts inside when the door closes; drives and soft starters need the clear space their maker gives above and below for air flow.

blocks.p: A tolerance is how far a position may be from the drawing and still be acceptable: 1 200 mm ± 3 mm means anything from 1 197 mm to 1 203 mm. A mark outside the tolerance is corrected before anything is fixed, never 'near enough'. Tight tolerances apply where items are seen together: a row of boxes, a line of lights, holes in a panel door.

sections.title: Setting out walls, ceilings and outdoor routes

flow: Mark and label the datum line round the room
Find the reference points: corners, openings, centre lines
Mark box centres and outlines from those references, using running dimensions
Check plumb and level, and the spacing between boxes in a row
Mark conduit and trunking routes: straight, plumb or level, clear of other services, and as short as practical
Mark fixing centres along each route
Check against the drawing, then have it checked by someone else

blocks.p: Marking the whole route on the wall before any saddle or fixing goes up lets you see that it is straight, clear of obstructions and other services, and as short as practical, and lets the checker see it too.

ul: Set out the room's two **centre lines** on the floor, at 90° to each other (check with 3-4-5 or equal diagonals), not just parallel to one wall that may be out of square.
Mark each light position on the floor from the centre lines, using the spacing worked out from the drawing.
Transfer each mark straight up to the ceiling with a plumb laser (or plumb bob). Most of the work is then done from the floor, which avoids much of the work at height.
Check the spacings on the ceiling against the drawing before any holes are drilled.
If a light falls on a beam or duct, do not move it yourself: record it and ask for a decision, because its position may have been chosen for light levels, alignment or other services.

flow: Study the site plan and records of existing services: water, sewer, telephone, power, gas
Ask the owner what they know, and scan the route with a cable and pipe detector
Mark any services found with paint or pegs; find the exact position of any that the route must keep a set distance from
Peg each end and run a string line between them; check distances
Set the route square to the building where needed (3-4-5)
Place offset pegs clear of the digging, and record tie measurements from fixed points
Mark the trench width and depth from the specification
Have the route checked before digging, and record it for the as-built drawing

blocks.p: **Offset pegs** are set a known distance to the side of a line or position, outside the area to be dug or driven over, so the position can be found again after the original pegs are disturbed. **Tie measurements** are distances from two fixed points (for example two corners of a building) to the position: where the two distances meet, the point is found again exactly.

blocks.note: Where the route crosses or runs near an existing service, its position is found by hand-digging a trial hole, not assumed from the drawing. Water pipes and old cables are often not where the plan shows them.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Marking out enclosures, gland plates and back plates

blocks.p: On an enclosure, the marking is the finished appearance: holes that are off-line or the wrong size are seen by everyone who uses the panel, and a door that will not close over the equipment inside has to be scrapped.

flow: Read the drawing and each device maker's cut-out and hole sizes; check them against the real devices
With the door closed, check that every door device will clear the parts inside
Take the door off and lay it flat on a clean, padded bench
Put masking tape where the holes will go, to protect the paint
Mark a vertical and a horizontal centre line from the datum edges
Mark each device's centre, and rectangles from their own centre lines
Have the marking checked against the drawing by a second person
Then punch lightly, drill pilot holes, and cut

ul: Use the **maker's cut-out size**, not the size of the device's front. A panel meter with a 96 mm × 96 mm front commonly needs a cut-out of about 92 mm × 92 mm, because the front must cover the edge of the hole.
Round devices often need a hole a little over their nominal size: '22 mm' push buttons commonly need about 22.3 mm to 22.5 mm, and some need an anti-rotation notch. Check the maker's sheet.

**Round holes:** light centre punch, small pilot hole, then open to size with a step drill or a **knockout punch**. A knockout punch needs a pilot hole for its **draw bolt**, which is tightened to pull the punch through the metal and gives a clean, burr-free hole.

**Rectangular holes:** drill a hole just inside each corner, touching the corner lines, then cut along the lines between them with a **nibbler** or a jigsaw with a metal-cutting blade, and file to the line.
Deburr every edge, remove the tape, clean off all swarf, and test-fit each device.
Remove the gland plate before marking and cutting it, so swarf does not fall into the enclosure onto terminals and electronics.
Space the hole centres so that each gland's locknut and a spanner can turn without hitting the next gland, and so that cables can bend into the panel.

Mark the hole size for the gland's thread and the maker's sheet (for example a clearance hole a little over the thread size). For conduit, remember that North American trade sizes do not match their names: a '½ inch' conduit knockout is about 22 mm across.

head: Item
Where and why
rows: Main isolator
Near where the incoming supply cable enters, so the unprotected cable inside the panel is short
Drives, soft starters and other heat sources
With the clear space their maker gives above and below, so air can flow; heat sources high in the panel, away from heat-sensitive items
DIN rails
Level, measured from a datum edge, with room between rows for trunking
Trunking
Between rows of devices, so wiring runs neatly and devices can be changed; power and control wiring kept apart where the specification asks
Terminal rails
Near the gland plate, so outgoing field cables are short and do not cross the panel
Spare space
Room for later additions, as the specification asks (often a set percentage)

blocks.p: Mark the clearances and trunking first, then the devices. Mark rail and trunking positions with a square and rule from the datum edge, have the layout checked, and only then drill. To mark holes that must line up with existing holes (for example a bracket on a frame), hold the part in place and mark through its holes.

blocks.note: Wear eye protection when drilling, punching and cutting; clamp the work, never hold it by hand; do not wear gloves near a turning drill; unplug power tools before changing bits or blades.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Checking, repeat work, leading the team and records

blocks.h: Check before you cut or drill

blocks.p: Every set-out is checked **before** anything is drilled, chased or cut. The best check is by a second competent person who did not do the marking, using the drawing and a **check sheet**: each item, its required position, its measured position, and pass or correct. People tend to repeat their own mistakes when they check their own work.

Where the same layout is repeated many times (identical houses on a scheme, identical rooms in a hotel or school), make a checked **template** or **story rod** (a straight rod or strip marked with the heights or positions), check it against the drawing, and use it everywhere. Every room then comes out the same, quickly. Check the template now and then for damage, and remember that a template cannot correct for a wall built in the wrong place.

ul: Make sure everyone has the same current revision of the drawings and the specification, and brief the team on the job, the datum and the heights.
Set (or check) **one datum** for the whole floor, so everyone works from the same reference and the same edge of the line.
Give each person a defined area, a checked height list and the team's marking and labelling system.
Walk round during the work and spot-check positions against the drawing.
Have each finished area checked by someone else with the check sheet, and correct any errors.
A constant error in one person's work (every box 25 mm high, for example) usually means they used a different reference: find it and put it right.
Only after the check is signed off does drilling start.

blocks.h: When the building does not match the drawing

flow: Stop marking the affected part
Recheck your own set-out: right reference, right revision?
Measure and photograph the difference
Report it to the supervisor, with possible options
Get a decision from the supervisor or designer
Mark the agreed change, tell the team and record it on the drawing

blocks.p: Do not quietly move items yourself. A light's position may have been chosen for the lighting level, to line up with other lights, or to clear air-conditioning ducts; an outlet may be placed for furniture or equipment the client has planned.

Every change agreed on site is marked on the drawing, with the date and who agreed it. These marked-up drawings become the **as-built (record) drawings**, which show how the installation was really built. They are vital for anyone who maintains, alters or drills into the building later.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can check that I have the current drawings, specification and schedules, and what to do when they disagree.
I can compare the site with the drawing and deal properly with a difference.
I can mark a datum line and work out every height from it, not from the rough floor.
I can choose between a spirit level, line laser, plumb laser, plumb bob, water level and chalk line, and check each is true.
I can make clear, labelled marks using running dimensions from one reference.
I can check for hidden services before drilling.
I can convert drawing measurements by scale and spot a copy printed at the wrong size.
I can work out equal spacing, fixing centres and centring.
I can set out a right angle with 3-4-5 and correct it from the diagonal.
I can work out conduit offsets and angles.
I can allow for plaster and tiles, and work out recess depths and tolerances.
I can set out a ceiling light grid from centre lines and transfer it up with a plumb laser.
I can set out an outdoor cable route with pegs, string lines, offset pegs and tie measurements.
I can mark out door cut-outs, gland plates and back plates from datum edges and makers' sizes.
I can describe how holes and rectangular cut-outs are made after marking.
I can lead a team set-out and organise an independent check before drilling.
I can record changes for the as-built drawings.

The straight edge of an enclosure or plate from which positions are measured.
The threaded bolt that pulls a knockout punch through sheet metal.
The level of the floor once screed and floor finishes are laid.

A tool that cuts a clean round hole in sheet metal, pulled through by a draw bolt.
A laser that projects a level or vertical line onto walls; self-levelling types set themselves.
A tool that cuts sheet metal by taking small bites along a line.
A peg set a known distance to the side of a position so it can be found again after digging.
Measuring every position from one reference point rather than from the previous mark.
In British practice, strips of wall in line with accessories, or near corners and ceilings, where hidden cables are expected.
The ratio between a drawing and real size, such as 1:50.
A straight strip marked with heights or positions, used to repeat a set-out quickly and the same each time.
Distances from two fixed points to a position, used to find it again exactly.
How far a position may be from the drawing and still be acceptable.
A clear tube filled with water, used to carry a level height round corners and between rooms.

c1.title: Setting out a health centre in Bath
c1.text: Kevin, a Level 3 electrician, is setting out boxes in a new health centre in Bath, St Thomas. The builder has painted 'FFL + 1 000' on each column, and Kevin has marked the datum line from it. The floor slab is still rough: 50 mm of screed and tiles will go on later. The specification gives switch centres at 1 250 mm and outlet centres at 400 mm above FFL. The drawings in Kevin's van are revision B; the site office holds revision C, issued last week. Along a 12 m corridor wall, six outlets are dimensioned from the corridor's end wall.

c2.title: A pump control panel for a Maggotty water scheme
c2.text: Sasha is marking out a steel enclosure for the pump control panel of a community water scheme in Maggotty, St Elizabeth. The door is 400 mm wide. A panel meter has a 96 mm × 96 mm front; the maker's sheet gives its cut-out as 92 mm × 92 mm (+0.8 mm). Three 22 mm push buttons go below it; the maker's sheet gives their hole as 22.3 mm. The back plate will carry a main isolator, a soft starter, DIN rails with trunking between them, and a terminal rail; all cables enter through a gland plate at the bottom.

c3.title: A gate-light trench at an Alligator Pond church
c3.text: Paulette is setting out a cable trench from the wall of a church in Alligator Pond, St Elizabeth, to a gate light 26 m away. The trench must leave the wall at 90°. She uses the 3-4-5 method, with 2.4 m measured along the wall and 3.2 m out along the trench line, both from the same corner point. She has also recorded tie measurements from two corners of the church to the gate-light peg.

c4.title: Lights and conduit in a Gordon Town hall
c4.text: A crew is setting out lights and conduit in a community hall in Gordon Town, St Andrew, which is 12 m long and 8 m wide. The drawing shows four lights in a row along the hall's centre line, with a full space at each end: the gap from each end wall to the nearest light equals the gap between lights. A concrete beam 120 mm deep crosses the ceiling, and the conduit must offset round it with two 30° bends. Kofi is marking the walls with a line laser, but the morning sun floods the walls through large windows.

c5.title: Leading a set-out on a New Kingston office floor
c5.text: Tamika, a Level 3 electrician, leads four members setting out boxes on one floor of an office block in New Kingston. She set one datum line round the floor and gave everyone a checked list of heights. On checking, she finds that every box Andre marked on the east side is exactly 25 mm higher than the drawing, while everyone else's are right. Andre has also scaled some positions off an A3 print of a drawing marked 'Scale 1:50 at A1'.

questions.q: Where is the centre of each outlet box marked, relative to Kevin's datum line?
o: 600 mm below the datum line
400 mm below the datum line
600 mm above the datum line
650 mm below the datum line
questions.why: The outlet centre is 400 mm above FFL and the datum is 1 000 mm above FFL, so the outlet is 1 000 − 400 = 600 mm below the datum. Measuring 400 mm up from the rough slab would put the box 650 mm below the datum: 50 mm too low once the screed and tiles are laid.

questions.q: What should Kevin do about the revision B drawings in his van?
o: Use revision B, as changes between revisions are usually small
Use whichever drawing shows more dimensions on it
Use revision C only, and take the old copies out of use
Mark from B now, and compare it with C at the end
questions.why: Work only from the current revision. A later revision may move boxes, add circuits or change heights, and setting out from an old drawing means re-marking or, worse, drilling in the wrong places. Mark old copies 'superseded' or remove them so nobody uses them by mistake.

questions.q: How should Kevin measure the positions of the six outlets along the corridor wall?
o: Each from the box before it, moving the tape along each time
All from the end wall, as the drawing gives them
Each from the nearest door frame, as it is easier
Space them by eye, then check only the last one
questions.why: Measuring every position from one reference (running dimensions) stops small errors adding up. Measuring each box from the one before carries every slip on, so the error grows along the wall. Door frames may not be where the drawing puts them, so they are poor references.

questions.q: What size should Sasha mark for the panel meter's cut-out?
o: 96 mm × 96 mm, the size of the meter's front
100 mm × 100 mm, to leave room to fit it
88 mm × 88 mm, so the front overlaps more
92 mm × 92 mm, from the maker's sheet
questions.why: The front (bezel) is bigger than the body so that it covers the edge of the hole. The maker's cut-out size, here 92 mm with a small plus tolerance, lets the body pass through and the clamps grip. A hole the size of the front would let the meter fall through.

questions.q: A push button will not go into a hole Sasha opened to 22 mm with a step drill. What is the best fix?
o: Force the button in, so that it grips the edge tightly
Open it to the maker's 22.3 mm with the right tool
File the button's thread down until it fits the hole
Drill a new 24 mm hole beside it and plug the first
questions.why: Device makers give the exact hole size, often a little over the nominal size, and sometimes a notch to stop the device turning. Check the maker's sheet before cutting, not just the nominal size. A hole slightly small can be opened carefully to size; forcing or filing the device damages it.

questions.q: If the meter cut-out is centred across the 400 mm door, how far from the door's left edge does it start?
o: 154 mm
200 mm
246 mm
152 mm
questions.why: Space left over = 400 − 92 = 308 mm, shared equally: 154 mm each side. Easier still, mark the door's centre line at 200 mm and measure 46 mm each way. 152 mm uses the meter's front instead of the cut-out; 246 mm is where the cut-out ends.

questions.q: Where on the back plate should the terminal rail be marked?
o: At the top, as far as possible from incoming cables
Beside the soft starter, so its heat keeps terminals dry
Near the gland plate, so field cables reach it easily
Anywhere there is space left when everything else is in
questions.why: Terminal rails go near where cables enter, so field cables are short and neat and do not cross the panel; the isolator also goes near the incoming supply. Heat sources such as soft starters need their maker's clearances for air flow, and a layout is planned, not filled in with leftovers.

questions.q: The diagonal between Paulette's two marks measures 4.08 m. What does this tell her?
o: Under 90°: swing the trench mark away from the wall mark
It is within 100 mm, so the angle is near enough square
The tape is wrong, as the diagonal can never be over 4 m
Over 90°: swing the trench mark towards the wall mark
questions.why: A 2.4–3.2 triangle is 3-4-5 × 0.8, so a right angle gives a 4.00 m diagonal. A longer diagonal means the angle is more than 90°, so the trench mark is swung round towards the wall mark, staying 3.2 m from the corner, until the diagonal is 4.00 m. Left as it is, the trench would be about 1 m off line at the gate.

questions.q: A delivery truck knocks out the gate-light peg before digging. How can Paulette find the exact spot again?
o: Re-measure both tie distances from the church corners
Measure 26 m from the wall in the general direction of the gate
Ask the delivery driver where the peg was before he hit it
Put a new peg where the grass looks a little flattened
questions.why: Tie measurements from two fixed points locate a spot exactly: where the two distances meet is the peg position. That is why set-outs record ties, or place offset pegs clear of digging and traffic. One distance and a rough direction can put the light well off its base.

questions.q: What is the spacing between the four lights?
questions.why: With a full space at each end, four lights make five equal gaps: 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 m, so the lights are at 2.4, 4.8, 7.2 and 9.6 m. 3.0 m would be right with half a space at each end, and 4.0 m if the end lights were on the walls.

questions.q: How far apart should the two 30° bends be marked on the conduit to clear the 120 mm beam?
o: 170 mm
120 mm
240 mm
208 mm
questions.why: Distance between bends = offset depth ÷ sin(bend angle). sin 30° = 0.5, so 120 ÷ 0.5 = 240 mm. 170 mm would suit 45° bends (× 1.41), and 208 mm uses the wrong trigonometric ratio. Allow a little extra depth if the conduit must clear the beam by a gap.

questions.q: Kofi can hardly see the line laser's beam on the sunny walls. What is the best answer?
o: Turn the laser on its side to make the beam look brighter
Mark the line by eye between the parts that he can see
Look straight into the laser to check whether it is on
Use a laser detector, or do that wall when it is shaded
questions.why: Line lasers are hard to see in bright sun. Most can be used with a hand-held detector that signals when it is on the beam, or the wall can be marked when it is in shade. Never guess the line by eye, and never look into the beam.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of Andre's boxes all being exactly 25 mm high?
o: He used a datum of his own, not the floor's datum
His tape measure stretches 25 mm when it is pulled tight
The floor on the east side is 25 mm lower than elsewhere
The boxes crept upwards while they were being fixed
questions.why: A constant error in every box from one person points to a different reference, such as a datum line he marked himself or a different edge of the line. That is why one datum is set for the whole floor and checked, and everyone measures from the same edge of it. Tapes and fixings give small, varying errors, not a steady 25 mm.

questions.q: Why are the positions Andre scaled from the A3 print wrong?
o: A3 prints are always made at exactly 1:50 by the printer
On A3 an A1 drawing is half size, so it is not 1:50
Scaling is wrong only on drawings over five years old
The scale holds, but A3 paper shrinks in the heat
questions.why: Printing A1 on A3 halves every length, so the print is really about 1:100, and anything scaled as 1:50 comes out half its true size. Use the written dimensions, or a scale bar printed on the drawing (which shrinks with the copy), and check a known dimension before scaling anything.

questions.q: Before any boxes are drilled, how should Tamika have the whole floor checked?
o: Each member checks his or her own marks once more at the end
She checks a few boxes at random, and then drilling starts
No check is needed, as everyone worked from one datum
Someone other than the marker checks each area on a sheet
questions.why: A second person, who did not mark the area, checks every position against the drawing with a check sheet before any drilling, because people tend to repeat their own mistakes when checking their own work. Spot checks help during the job but do not replace a full check, as Andre's error shows.

questions.q: A kitchen wall will get 6 mm of tile adhesive and 8 mm tiles over the finished plaster. How far should an outlet box stand out from the plaster so it finishes flush with the tiles?
o: 8 mm
6 mm
14 mm
2 mm
questions.why: The box front must end up level with the finished surface: 6 + 8 = 14 mm beyond the plaster. Set it short and the outlet plate sits in a hole; set it proud and the plate rocks. Extension rings can correct small errors, but it is better to mark and fix the box right.

questions.q: Five floodlight brackets go along a 14 m wall, the first and last each 1 m from the ends of the wall and the rest equally spaced between them. What is the spacing?
questions.why: The distance from the first bracket to the last is 14 − 1 − 1 = 12 m, and five brackets make four gaps: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.0 m. Count the gaps, not the brackets: items in a row with one at each end have one gap fewer than items.

questions.q: You must cut chases in a block wall along marked routes with a wall chaser. Which control matters most for your lungs?
o: Working fast, so the dust has less time to build up in the room
Dust extraction on the tool, plus a proper dust mask
Opening a window and working on regardless
A cotton cloth tied over the nose and mouth
questions.why: Cutting block and concrete gives off fine silica dust, which can cause lasting lung disease. Control it at the source with on-tool extraction (or water), and wear the respiratory protection the risk assessment names, with eye protection. A cloth or an open window does not stop the fine dust.

questions.q: How can you check that a spirit level reads true before marking a long trunking route?
o: Lay it on the new floor slab, which is always truly level
Hold it against a door frame, which is always plumb
Check the bubble is in the vial, which proves it is true
Read it, turn it end for end on the same spot, compare
questions.why: Place the level on a firm surface, read the bubble, turn it end for end on exactly the same spot and read again. If the bubble sits in the same place both ways, the level is true; if not, have it adjusted or replaced. Floors and door frames are not reliable references.

questions.q: A row of eight boxes must be level within ±3 mm. Why mark them from a laser line rather than by moving a 600 mm spirit level from box to box?
o: A spirit level cannot be used on a block wall at all
A laser line is wider, so the boxes are easier to hit
Small errors at each move of the level add up
Spirit levels work only on horizontal surfaces, not walls
questions.why: Each time a short level is moved along, its own small error and your reading error are added to the last, and over eight boxes they can exceed 3 mm. A laser line or a datum line gives every box the same reference at once.
